summary: Tricholine citrate is a choline derivative (the citrate salt providing choline) used as a lipotropic and hepatic-support / appetite-supporting agent. It is NOT approved by the US FDA and is used predominantly in India and parts of Asia, usually as an ingredient in combination syrups and tonics (frequently with sorbitol, and in paediatric formulations with cyproheptadine as an appetite stimulant); the information here is therefore based on product literature and pharmacology rather than an FDA label. Choline is an essential nutrient and a precursor for membrane phospholipids (such as phosphatidylcholine) and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, and it has a lipotropic role in hepatic fat metabolism and bile (it contributes a mild choleretic effect). Tricholine citrate is generally well tolerated, with mild gastrointestinal effects being the most common complaint. It should not be used as a substitute for proper evaluation of the cause of poor appetite or weight loss, and robust clinical-efficacy evidence is limited.

moa: Tricholine citrate supplies choline, an essential nutrient. Choline is incorporated into membrane phospholipids (notably phosphatidylcholine) and is the precursor of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine and of betaine. As a lipotropic factor, choline participates in the mobilisation and metabolism of hepatic fat (assisting the export of triglycerides as very-low-density lipoprotein and reducing fatty accumulation), and it exerts a mild choleretic effect promoting bile flow. In the combination tonics in which it is commonly used, the appetite-stimulating effect is generally attributed to the co-formulated agent (e.g. cyproheptadine), while tricholine citrate provides the lipotropic/hepatic-support component.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to the product or any of its components
relative: Use of combination products in patients for whom a co-ingredient (e.g. cyproheptadine) is contraindicated
Pregnancy and lactation (use only on clinician advice)
Unexplained weight loss or poor appetite that has not been evaluated
monitor: Adverse effects attributable to combination ingredients

preg: There are limited data specific to tricholine citrate in pregnancy. Choline is a required nutrient in pregnancy, but the supportive/combination products containing tricholine citrate should be used during pregnancy only if advised by a clinician, particularly because co-ingredients may carry their own cautions.
lact: There are limited data specific to tricholine citrate during breastfeeding. Use only if advised by a clinician, taking into account any co-formulated ingredients.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is established. Use with general caution; there are no robust data in significant renal impairment.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is established. Lipotropic agents have a theoretical supportive role in hepatic fat metabolism, but there are no robust data to guide dosing in hepatic impairment.

major: No clinically significant major interactions established for tricholine citrate itself

interactions.diagnostics: No known clinically significant laboratory interference

pearls: Tricholine citrate is NOT FDA-approved; it is used mainly in India/Asia, usually as a component of combination syrups - this record is based on product literature, not an FDA label.
It is a choline-providing lipotropic/choleretic agent; choline is a precursor of phospholipids and acetylcholine.
In paediatric appetite tonics it is commonly combined with cyproheptadine (the actual appetite stimulant) and sorbitol - check the full formulation and the cautions of each ingredient.
High-quality efficacy evidence is limited; it is supportive and should not delay evaluation of the underlying cause of anorexia or weight loss.
It is generally well tolerated, with mild gastrointestinal upset the most common effect.
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered, or skip it if it is almost time for the next dose - do not double the dose. As a supportive tonic, an occasional missed dose is not harmful.
overdose: Tricholine citrate has low acute toxicity; overdose would most likely cause gastrointestinal upset such as nausea, abdominal discomfort, and diarrhoea (very high choline intake can cause sweating, a fishy body odour, and a fall in blood pressure). There is no specific antidote; manage supportively with hydration and symptomatic care. With combination products, consider and manage the effects of any co-ingredients (e.g. cyproheptadine).
